structure.title: I.A-C Institutional background: pension system, framing, budget constraint discontinuities
V Retirement bunching and reference points in a simple model
VI Structural bunching estimation and counterfactuals

observations.statement: The paper frames its central estimand as the direct behavioral effect of statutory retirement ages on bunching, net of underlying financial incentives, formalized as coefficients on statutory-age type dummies in a discontinuity-level regression.
observations.locator: Section II.B and Section III.B, equations (3) and (5)

observations.statement: Two explicit, numbered identifying assumptions (labeled Assumption A and Assumption B) are stated, requiring that structural elasticities not vary systematically with the presence of a statutory age, at the pooled and within-group level respectively.
observations.quote: structural elasticities do not vary systematically

observations.statement: The authors discuss as a threat to identification that observed differences in bunching across discontinuity types could reflect systematic differences in underlying financial-incentive elasticities rather than a genuine statutory-age effect, motivating the stated assumptions.

The approach is named as a multi-discontinuity extension of the standard bunching estimator, distinguishing threshold-specific observed elasticities from structural parameters recovered by pooling many bunching observations in one regression.

Identification of bunching itself rests on an explicitly stated assumption that the retirement-age density would have been smooth absent the threshold, noted before the excess-mass formula is derived.

The main data source is named as administrative records from the German State Pension Fund covering the population of pension claimants, supplemented for part of the analysis by a household survey panel providing occupation-level variables.

The birth-cohort window used for the main analysis is stated explicitly, with the justification that only cohorts whose retirement-age distribution is fully observed within the data window are retained.

Several sample exclusions are each justified individually in the text, including dropping workers who continue employment after claiming a pension, excluding early post-reunification East German retirees because of a distinct benefit-calculation regime, and requiring a minimum contribution history.

The paper distinguishes three units of observation used across different parts of the analysis: an individual-level sample, an occupation-matched sample, and a discontinuity-level bunching sample used for the main regressions.
The underlying administrative data are described as accessed through a research data center rather than distributed as a public-use file, consistent with restricted-access administrative microdata.

The summary statistics table reports the number of observations separately for each of the three samples used, with the discontinuity-level sample reported alongside the two worker-level samples for comparison.

The outcome analyzed throughout is the monthly job-exit (retirement) age, which the authors note is imputed from insurance-status information when the timing of the last pension contribution does not coincide with the last employment spell.

The key regressors are indicator variables for the presence of each type of statutory retirement age at a discontinuity and a continuous kink-size variable defined as the local change in the implicit net-of-tax rate.

The dependent variable in the discontinuity-level regressions is excess bunching mass normalized by the threshold retirement age rather than raw excess mass, so that the measure is comparable across discontinuities located at different ages.
Lifetime-income and budget-constraint variables underlying the simulation are discounted to present value using a stated discount rate and stated cohort-specific life expectancy assumptions.
The main results table lists which fixed effects (pathway, year-of-birth, and their interaction) are included in each column as separate labeled rows rather than describing them only in a footnote.

Columns of the main table progressively add statutory-age interactions, worker-level controls, group fixed effects, and occupation-level controls, moving from a bare bivariate specification to fully saturated ones.

The table reports the number of discontinuity-level observations underlying each column and notes that the count falls in later columns because of missing occupation-level data or insufficient within-group variation for heterogeneous-coefficient specifications.
An R-squared statistic is reported for every column of the main results table alongside the coefficient estimates.
The table notes state that all regressions are weighted by group size and that reported standard errors are obtained by a bootstrap procedure rather than an analytic formula.

Standard errors throughout the discontinuity-level regressions are computed via a bootstrap that resamples bunching observations, mentioned in a single sentence without further justification for why a bootstrap rather than an analytic standard error is used at this level.

For the specific-discontinuity comparison figures earlier in the results section, standard errors shown in parentheses are described only as bootstrapped, with no separate discussion of the inference method for those particular estimates.

The paper does not discuss clustering of standard errors at any level, such as by pathway or birth-cohort group, consistent with treating each discontinuity as the unit of a cross-sectional regression rather than as a panel with repeated group observations.

The paper compares the shape of the pooled empirical retirement-age density around statutory ages against the density predicted by the reference-dependence model and by a rival behavioral model, using the presence or absence of missing mass on one side of the threshold as the distinguishing test.

Additional diagnostic exercises, including density comparisons split by statutory-age type and sensitivity of heterogeneity results to alternative residualization controls, are reported only in the online appendix rather than the main text.
observations.locator: text references to online Appendix Figures A5 and A12

observations.statement: Two policy reforms are used as quasi-diagnostic checks on the proposed mechanism, examining whether bunching shifts in lockstep with a gradually phased statutory-age change and whether increased information-letter frequency shifts bunching toward the age emphasized in the letters.

The main reduced-form table itself functions as a robustness exercise, showing that estimated statutory-age effects remain qualitatively stable as fixed effects, worker controls, and occupation-level controls are added successively.

Separate specifications allow parameters to vary by pathway, birth cohort, and their interaction, and the text reports that the direct statutory-age effect persists within these more narrowly defined groups.

Robustness of the structural reference-dependence parameter estimates to alternative functional forms and to estimating each statutory-age type separately is reported in an online appendix table rather than in the main text.
observations.locator: text reference to online Appendix Table A7

observations.statement: A decomposition exercise is used as an additional robustness check to gauge how much of the difference in bunching across discontinuity types can be attributed to observable worker and firm characteristics versus an unexplained component.
observations.locator: Section III.C footnote, online Appendix Table A1

observations.statement: Heterogeneity in observed bunching elasticities is reported by sorting discontinuities into quintiles of residualized worker and occupation characteristics after first partialling out other observables via an auxiliary regression.

The heterogeneity analysis is framed as a check on the identifying assumption and on alternative behavioral mechanisms, such as financial sophistication and firm-driven layoffs, rather than as a policy-relevant treatment-effect heterogeneity exercise in its own right.

Results from heterogeneity by financial-sophistication proxies are explicitly described as sensitive to the choice of control variables used in the residualizing regression, with this caveat stated directly rather than left implicit.

A gradual, cohort-by-cohort phase-in of a statutory-age reform is used as a natural experiment, showing that the location of bunching tracks the monthly statutory-age schedule throughout the transition period.
Evidence on the effect of increased information-letter frequency on bunching at the associated statutory age is explicitly described by the authors as suggestive rather than conclusive.

The authors examine whether employer-driven layoff incentives can explain the statutory-age effect by comparing bunching among self-employed workers and workers in firms exempt from employment-protection rules to the full sample, concluding that firm responses do not appear to be the primary driver.

Correlational checks using individual-level regressions of the probability of bunching at a statutory age on socioeconomic proxies for financial literacy and liquidity are used as mechanism evidence against two specific alternative explanations.

The estimated retirement-age elasticity with respect to financial incentives is explicitly benchmarked against elasticities from prior studies that use different institutional settings and data sources.

The fiscal consequences of the two simulated pension reforms are summarized through an explicit back-of-the-envelope calculation expressed in monetary terms and compared directly across the two policy scenarios.

The authors explicitly note when an estimated structural parameter is precisely estimated relative to the other parameters recovered in the same specification, rather than reporting only point estimates.

The conclusion explicitly states that the paper remains agnostic about the welfare consequences of policies that manipulate statutory ages, since evaluating welfare would require a normative stance on how reference-point effects should enter welfare calculations.

The authors state that the role of liquidity constraints at the early retirement age cannot be fully verified because no data on individual assets are available, and note this as a reason for narrowing the structural interpretation to later statutory ages.
The paper's opening figure presents a raw, unsmoothed count of job exits by monthly age bin for the full sample as the first piece of descriptive evidence.
A binned-scatterplot format is used to summarize the relationship between excess mass and kink size separately for statutory-age and pure-financial-incentive discontinuities.
A dedicated summary statistics table reports means and standard deviations of key variables across the three samples used in the paper, each corresponding to a different unit of observation.
Table and figure notes consistently spell out the estimation sample, the weighting scheme, and the type of standard error underlying the reported numbers.
The introduction closes with an explicit roadmap paragraph naming each numbered section of the paper and describing its content in order.
observations.quote: Section I outlines context and data

observations.statement: The introduction contains an explicit, numbered statement of the paper's main contributions before turning to the literature review.
The institutional background and data section is presented before the empirical methodology section, rather than leading with the estimating equation.

Mechanism evidence is presented in a dedicated section placed after the main reduced-form results and before the structural model, establishing the effect first and investigating why it arises afterward.

The introduction previews the paper's main qualitative results, that financial incentives alone cannot explain retirement bunching and that statutory ages have a direct effect, before the corresponding sections are reached.
The reference list includes a formal citation to a deposited replication data package for this paper, hosted through a data archive distinct from the journal itself.

A title-page footnote directs readers to the journal's article page for additional materials and an author disclosure statement, while the underlying administrative dataset is described as obtained through a research data center rather than distributed with the paper.

Survey data are merged onto the administrative pension records at an aggregated occupation level to add worker and firm characteristics not available in the administrative source, producing what the paper calls an occupation-matched sample.

The paper notes that the magnitude of the simulated fiscal effect from shifting statutory ages depends on features specific to the pension system's own benefit-adjustment schedule, flagging a limit on extrapolating the fiscal simulation to other institutional settings.

The counterfactual simulation extrapolates estimated parameters to a policy change and a birth cohort beyond those directly used for estimation, and the authors flag the implicit assumption underlying this extrapolation.

concordance.note: The dataset name RTZN is consistent with the German pension-entry ('Rentenzugang') administrative data described in the paper, though the card does not itself state the fund name.

gaps: No explicit McCrary-style density manipulation test is reported for the running variable used in the bunching estimation itself, distinct from the density-shape comparison used later to discriminate between behavioral models.

No formal pre-analysis plan, IRB approval, or consent statement is mentioned anywhere in the main text; the setting uses administrative data rather than a survey or experiment where such statements are typical.
No explicit clustering of standard errors by pathway, cohort, or any other group is discussed; only a bootstrap over bunching observations is described, without stating the resampling unit.
The main text does not name the statistical software used to produce the estimates or figures.
No formal weak-instrument, first-stage, or overidentification diagnostic appears, consistent with the paper not using an instrumental-variables design.

reading.note: Read the entire extracted text line by line from the abstract through the reference list (pages 1-40), including all footnotes and table/figure notes. Page 41 is a blank trailing page with no content. The paper repeatedly points to a separate online appendix (Appendix Tables A1-A7, Figures A1-A13, Sections B-G) that is not part of this extracted text and was not read; observations note explicitly where the paper defers detail to that appendix.
